## Overview

The Integrated Postsecondary Education Data System (IPEDS) is the
annual census of U.S. postsecondary institutions, collected by the
National Center for Education Statistics (NCES). Reporting is mandatory
for institutions that participate in Title IV federal student aid
programs, which is most of the universe — 5,837 of the 6,163
institutions in the 2023–24 collection. The rest are reported but do
not currently participate in Title IV. Because the collection covers a
universe rather than a sample, it is not subject to sampling error.

That universe is shrinking. IPEDS carried 7,503 institutions in 2010 and
6,072 in 2024.

IPEDS is not a single table. It is a set of component surveys, each
collected on its own schedule and at its own grain: institutional
characteristics, completions, graduation rates, enrollment, finance,
staffing, student financial aid and outcome measures. Each component is
released provisionally and then reissued as a revised file the
following year.

What makes IPEDS usable for place-based research is that every record
is keyed to an institution whose address and county, along with its
sector, level and control, are reported in the directory file. That
allows awards, headcounts and completion outcomes to be aggregated from
institutions to counties — turning an institution-level census into a
measure of local postsecondary capacity.

::: callout-note
IPEDS measures **production**, not attainment. A degree is credited to
the county where the institution sits, not where the student lives. In
communities where students commute to a metro campus, or enroll online,
local educational attainment and local degree production can diverge
sharply.
:::

## What this data tells us about rural America

Rural colleges and universities are assets, and IPEDS is the record of
where they are and what they produce. They do three kinds of work for a
rural economy at once.

**They are anchor institutions.** A college can be among the largest
employers in its county, with a payroll and a physical footprint that do
not relocate. It also tends to supply arts, athletics, lectures and
public spaces that a rural county might otherwise lack.

**They are talent development engines.** They produce the credentials
that raise local educational attainment. Where a rural county has an
active institution, it has a mechanism for building human capital in
place rather than importing it.

**They are economic development partners.** Rural institutions skew
toward career-focused programs tied to local industry — the two-year
colleges, regional publics and small privates that make up most of the
rural landscape. That orientation makes them practical partners for
workforce strategy, and a connection point between graduates and the
capital and employers in the wider economy.

Their footprint is often regional rather than county-shaped. In rural
areas access frequently depends on drive time, and an institution may
draw students, employ staff and place graduates across more than one
county. County boundaries cut through that footprint in both
directions: a county counted as having no institution may be well
served by a neighbor, and a college town's degree production is
credited entirely to the host county even though the capacity serves
the region.

IPEDS also identifies what kind of asset each institution is. It
distinguishes public from private nonprofit and private for-profit,
four-year from two-year and less-than-two-year, and degree-granting from
non-degree-granting.

IPEDS carries its own geographic classification as well. Each
institution is assigned an NCES urban-centric locale code, which
separates city, suburb, town and rural settings and further splits rural
into fringe, distant and remote — useful for distinguishing an
institution in a rural county adjacent to a metro area from one serving
a genuinely remote region.

Because completions are reported by program code, IPEDS also joins to
occupational data through the NCES CIP-to-SOC crosswalk — the step that
turns degree counts into a measure of occupational supply, and a local
institution into a legible workforce asset.

::: callout-note
**What this data cannot answer.** The components curated here cover
institutions, awards and completion outcomes — not enrollment. Headcount
by level, and online and distance education, live in the IPEDS
Enrollment (`EF`) component, which is not included. Coverage also begins
in 2010; longer historical series have to be pulled from the source
files directly.
:::

## Coverage

- **Geography:** Institution; aggregable to county via the institution
  directory

- **Time range:** The IPEDS Data Center distributes files back to 1980,
  the earliest of them from collections that predate IPEDS itself. CORI's
  curation covers 2010–present, the period over which award-level and
  geographic coding are consistent enough for cross-year comparison

- **Update frequency:** Annual. Provisional files release in the summer
  following the collection year, with revised files about a year later

- **Universe:** The IPEDS universe of postsecondary institutions —
  6,163 in 2023–24, of which 5,837 participate in Title IV federal
  student aid programs and are required to report. Counts have declined
  from 7,503 in 2010

- **Component surveys curated by CORI:** Institutional Characteristics
  (`HD`), Completions awards (`C_A`), Completions completers (`C_C`),
  Graduation Rates (`GR`)

::: callout-note
**Release lags differ by component.** Graduation rates publish roughly a
year behind the others, so the most recent IPEDS vintage typically has
institutional characteristics and completions but no completion
outcomes. The completers file begins in 2012 — NCES published none
before that. Neither gap is an error in the data; both are properties of
the collection schedule.
:::

## Key variables

**Institutional capacity**

- Counts of degree-granting institutions, by control (public, private
  nonprofit) and level (four-year, two-year)
- Counts of HBCUs and tribal colleges
- Institution directory: sector, level, control, Carnegie
  classification, urbanization level, enrollment size category,
  land-grant and HBCU status

**Degrees conferred**

- Total degrees conferred, associate through doctoral
- Share of degrees by level and by sex
- At institution level: awards by 6-digit CIP program code, award level
  and major number

**Student headcounts**

- Students completing, by award level (2012 onward)

**Completion outcomes**

- Six-year graduation rate for the four-year full-time first-time
  bachelor's-seeking cohort
- Transfer-out rate

Award counts and student headcounts answer different questions and are
not interchangeable. The Completions file counts *awards*; the
completers file counts *students*. A student who earns two degrees at
the same level counts as two awards but one completer, and the gap
concentrates at the associate level, where degrees run roughly 10% ahead
of students.

::: callout-note
**Three NCES conventions inflate a naive sum** of the institution-level
completions table. CIP code `99.0000` is each institution's grand total
across programs, included alongside the per-program rows. `major_num`
of 2 is a double-majoring student's second major. And certificates are
not degrees — the award level column spans certificates through
doctorates. Together the first two inflate a 2024 national degree count
from 4.14 million to 8.46 million.
:::

## Accessing the data

### Via CORI R package

The [`cori.data.ipeds`](/packages/cori-data-ipeds/) package provides
tidy access to four IPEDS files at both the county and institution
levels, with canonical column names, NCES sentinel codes converted to
`NA`, and the value labels for every categorical column carried in the
codebook.

```r
library(cori.data.ipeds)

# County level — tidy long
get_institutions(geoids = "33009", years = 2024)
get_degrees(geoids = "33009", years = 2024)
get_completers(geoids = "33009", years = 2024)
get_graduation_rates(geoids = "33009", years = 2012:2023)

# Institution level — wide, with CIP detail
get_degrees(geography = "institution", geoids = "33009", years = 2024)

# Variable definitions, coverage caveats and value labels
get_ipeds_codebook()

# Map programs to occupations
get_cip_soc_crosswalk("2020")
```

### Direct from source

Annual CSV files for every component are available as zip archives from
the [IPEDS Data Center](https://nces.ed.gov/ipeds/datacenter/DataFiles.aspx),
organized by survey and year. Each file comes with a dictionary workbook
whose Frequencies sheet carries the value labels for its categorical
columns. The [CIP resources page](https://nces.ed.gov/ipeds/cipcode/resources.aspx)
hosts the CIP taxonomy and the CIP-to-SOC crosswalks.

- **Package:** [cori.data.ipeds](/packages/cori-data-ipeds/) — CORI's
  tidy access layer, with county aggregations and the CIP-to-SOC
  crosswalk
- **Package:** [cori.data](/packages/cori-data/) — meta-package
  including `cori.data.ipeds`
- **Dataset:** [Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages](/datasets/qcew-employment-wages/)
  — IPEDS describes the talent a place produces; QCEW describes the jobs
  available to absorb it
- **Dataset:** [American Community Survey](/datasets/american-community-survey/)
  — resident educational attainment, which diverges from local degree
  production wherever students commute or leave
- **Dataset:** [Census Population Estimates](/datasets/census-population-estimates/)
  — the denominator for per-resident degree production
